entries.title: Blackhawks have Stanley Cup-sized hole at centennial game
entries.summary: <p>No city in the nation, dare I say the world, celebrates its sports history as Chicago does.</p><p>Players from the 1985 Bears are still celebrated as though they won the Super Bowl last year. The 1969 Cubs didn’t even make the playoffs, and they might be the second-most celebrated team in the franchise’s 150-year history. The 1983 White Sox remain a fan favorite, and they lost in the playoffs.</p><p>On Tuesday at the United Center, the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" > Blackhawks</a> capped a yearlong celebration of their 100-year existence with a centennial game against the Maple Leafs, the same franchise they played in their first game on Nov. 17, 1926. Love the symmetry.</p><p>And before the game, the Hawks’ five ambassadors — Denis Savard, Chris Chelios, Pat Foley, Jeremy Roenick and Eddie Olczyk — participated in a Q&A with fans, telling stories from their time with the team. Love the group.</p><p>But the night was so Chicagoy and Hawksy. History is the only thing Hawks fans have to celebrate. Today stinks as bad as when the elephants in the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus would leave their muck around Chicago Stadium, speaking of history.</p><p>The Hawks entered the game in the same neighborhood they’ve inhabited the last four seasons, in the bottom three of the league, with the playoffs a pipe dream. They’ve been mocked on NHL broadcaster TNT, and their methods have been questioned by hockey media.</p><p>Let’s celebrate!</p><p>If the Hawks wanted to celebrate something, why not have players from those three Stanley Cup-winning teams in the 2010s — it feels like a generation ago — participate in the pomp and circumstance of the centennial game?</p><p>Nothing against the five ambassadors — my first hockey sweater was Savard’s, I had a poster with Chelios and Roenick (“Black Reign” — if you know, you know) and Foley and Olczyk formed the best TV duo in hockey — but where was the Cup representation?</p><p>Were the Hawks celebrating 100 years or just the 1980s and 90s?</p><p>Chelios might’ve played his best hockey with the Hawks, but he won two Cups with the Red Wings and was booed relentlessly when he’d return home, even after his career. Remember when he said, “Come on, guys, let bygones be bygones” in 2010? He got back in fans’ good graces in the last few years, and his number was retired in 2024.</p><p>“There’s still one thing missing on my résumé, and that’s a Stanley Cup with the Blackhawks,” Chelios said at the Q&A. “Thankfully, I’m part of the organization. I’m hoping I’m with you drinking out of that Cup, bringing it to Murphy’s and Mount Carmel with the right team this time.”</p><p>Brilliant pandering.</p><p>Savard also won a Cup elsewhere, with the Canadiens. The Hawks traded him there to get Chelios. Two players traded for each other who won Cups elsewhere. Roenick never won a Cup in his five-team, 20-year career, coming closest with the 1992 Hawks, who lost in the Final.</p><p>Worst of all, the Hawks pushed Foley and Olczyk out of the TV booth together in arguably the most ridiculous decision in Chicago sports broadcasting history. Talk about letting bygones be bygones, they’ve graciously returned to the organ-i-zation, despite the bitter taste left by their departures, and have reconnected with adoring fans.</p><p>Speaking of those fans, they still have the Hawks in the top half of the league in attendance. Thanks to them, it’s hard to see a return to the dark ages of the 2000s, when the franchise made itself irrelevant and crowds dwindled to an average of less than 13,000 per game.</p><p>The Hawks have connected with kids at local rinks and have hosted them in their own. Despite all the losing, the team has cultivated a solid fan base. But there are cracks, and they tend to grow and make noise when things go bad, as they are now.</p><p>Those 2000s were no fun for anyone. If you attended games then, you’ll recall easy in-and-out parking, short lines at concession stands and in bathrooms and lousy hockey. The Hawks shouldn’t tempt fate with more years of lousy hockey.</p><p>The NHL made a nice gesture by acknowledging its teams celebrating centennials with Original Six matchups this week, all nationally televised. In addition to Leafs-Hawks, the Rangers hosted the Canadiens on Monday, and the Red Wings will host the Bruins on Wednesday.</p><p>The NHL reveres its founding teams more than any other U.S. league. Players acknowledge how special it is to play for them. When those teams play well, the league does well.</p><p>The Hawks are not playing well, and who knows when they will. With a painful present, the only thing they have going for them is their past. But at some point, the past gets old, too.</p>

entries.title: CPS and principals union reach tentative agreement that raises pay, brings back some positions
entries.summary: <p>After two years of bargaining, the union that represents Chicago Public Schools principals has reached a tentative contract agreement with the district that would guarantee 3% raises for the next three years and restore dozens of district-funded assistant principal positions at smaller schools.</p><p>The district and the Chicago Principals and Administrators Association, which represents nearly 1,200 principals and assistant principals, announced the agreement last week and issued more details Monday.</p><p>Union members will vote by Thursday on whether to ratify the contract and then it will go before the Chicago School Board for final approval next month.</p><p>It’s the first union contract for school leaders in Illinois and a victory for Chicago administrators who fought for years to have more of a voice on district policies and their working conditions.</p><p>Under the proposed deal, school leaders would receive a 3% raise this school year and in each of the next two school years. The two sides had previously agreed to 4% raises for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years, pending a full contract.</p><p>The agreement also includes measures to keep assistant principals at smaller schools, after CPS said it would no longer fund those positions earlier this year, and makes changes to the discipline and grievance procedures. The union had previously <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2023/08/01/chicago-public-schools-aggressive-tactics-for-removing-principals-under-the-microscope" target="_blank" ><u>accused the district of failing to give due process</u></a> to principals under scrutiny for alleged wrongdoing.</p><p>Kia Banks, the president of the principals union, said that was a major focus for the union in negotiations.</p><p>“Due process was the reason we fought to unionize,” Banks told the Sun-Times and WBEZ Tuesday.</p><p>She added that union leadership sought to fight against “unfair discipline that school leaders were subjected to mostly because of a lack of resources and support from management.” In the past, Banks said, some school leaders were disciplined before CPS completed an investigation.</p><p>Union and district leaders celebrated the deal in a joint statement.</p><p>CPS Supt. Macquline King said the tentative agreement represented a “vital step forward in honoring and supporting the leaders who make a lasting impact in our schools.”</p><p>Other highlights of the agreement include a $6,000 bonus for principals who’ve received a “proficient” or “distinguished” rating who sign back-to-back contract renewals at their school, which usually means they’ve stayed for at least eight years.</p><p>It also “guarantees” due process for principals accused of violating policies, the union said, and says that union members may be disciplined or fired “only for just cause.”</p><p>Banks said while union members don’t oppose “fair discipline or accountability and responsibility,” before this agreement “there was no onus on management to do that in a fair and just way.”</p><p>School leaders can also appeal “severe discipline,” and suspensions and written reprimands can be removed from an administrator’s record after three years.</p><p>Talks between the principals union and the district stalled as CPS negotiated with the Chicago Teachers Union on their contract in 2024 and 2025.</p><p>But negotiations seemed to acquire a new sense of urgency earlier this year after the district <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/13/as-cps-cuts-staff-to-plug-deficit-educator-unions-and-school-board-members-press-for-more-state-funding" target="_blank" ><u>announced that it would cut funding </u></a>for assistant principals at some schools to help plug a $732 million budget deficit. At the time, Banks said the union would pursue “all legal action” to maintain those positions.</p><p>Most of the schools that would have been affected by the planned cuts ended up using discretionary dollars to keep their assistant principals, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/07/chicago-public-schools-cuts-assistant-principal-funding/?link_source=ta_first_comment&taid=6a52e71df90d430001cc7039&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_medium=social&utm_source=facebook" target="_blank" ><u>according to Chalkbeat Chicago</u></a>.</p><p>The new agreement restores district-funded assistant principal positions at schools with 200 to 249 students, according to the union. The deal also establishes a joint district and union committee that will review how assistant principals are allocated.</p><p>Union contracts for principals are uncommon because school leaders are generally classified as managers under state labor laws which exclude them from collective bargaining rights. In Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2023/01/06/bill-giving-chicago-principals-bargaining-rights-is-headed-to-governors-desk" target="_blank" ><u>that changed in 2023</u></a> when principals won union representation rights under a law that also reclassified them as supervisors instead of managers.</p><p>Other school districts where principals are unionized include New York City, San Diego and Denver.</p>

entries.title: A tale of two Calebs: How Williams and Wilson got their names
entries.summary: <p>What do Caleb Williams and Caleb Wilson have in common, besides holding the hopes of nearly 3 million Chicagoans in their hands?</p><p>It goes deeper than just the first name — it’s the biblical roots.</p><p>On Tuesday after Bears practice, Williams told reporters that his parents, Carl and Dayna, chose his name from the Book of Numbers. Funny enough, Wilson’s parents, Jerry and Sabrina, had the same idea.</p><p>“My parents were in church one day and they were reading a story in the Bible about Caleb, and it resonated with them,” Wilson told the Sun-Times earlier this month. “They felt like [overcoming adversity] was going to be a theme in my life. And it really has been.”</p><p>In the Bible story, Caleb is one of 12 leaders sent by Moses to assess the Promised Land. Caleb’s compatriots return from the expedition ready to abandon God’s direction, overcome with doubts about their ability to conquer the land. Caleb goes against the grain: he urges his people not to be afraid and to trust that God is on their side.</p><p>It’s a fitting story for two athletes so willing to present themselves as figures of change for franchises that had been stagnating.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/17/bears-qb-caleb-williams-pete-crow-armstrongs-mvp-a-celebration-for-chicago-sports-friend-group" >Bears QB Caleb Williams: Pete Crow-Armstrong’s MVP a celebration for Chicago sports ‘friend group’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>That inner resolve started paying off for Williams last season. Gone were the days of using Bears games as the most efficient window to do my Sunday grocery shopping — their comebacks had become a sight to behold.</p><p>I remember watching in disbelief at the end of the Rams game as Williams sprinted backward, doing what you are surely taught not to do at quarterback school, and firing a “fadeaway jumper,” as the announcer called it, 60 yards downfield.</p><p>When it landed in tight end Cole Kmet’s hands in the end zone, I felt the ripple effects of awe: an inner turning, a hopeful glow extended to all my own problems.</p><p>The Bears ended up losing in overtime, but when the Bulls drafted Wilson with the fourth overall pick this past summer, the feeling solidified: a new era was dawning in Chicago. Not only did we have Williams, the comeback king, now we had the most talented Bull since Derrick Rose.</p><p>Or at the very least, the bounciest Bull.</p><p>“We’re both going to do great things for the city,” Wilson said. “[Williams] has already started winning. It’s just up to me now to bring that too.”</p><p>Easier said than done<b>.</b> Despite his high-flying dunks and surprisingly smooth 3-pointers, Wilson is no longer able to single-handedly take over games like he did in college. The Bulls began the season 1-9, and that was before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/11/12/bulls-losing-demoralizing-understanding-process" >Wilson broke his hand.</a></p><p>It’s a struggle Williams knows well.</p><p>“We are going through very similar situations with him going to a team and they’re not doing as well right now, and that was my first year,” Williams said Tuesday. “We didn’t win as many games as we wanted to.”</p><p>Williams' choppy path to the top of the football world might be reason enough to hold out hope for Wilson. Wilson certainly doesn’t think it’s a coincidence that they’re here together at the same time.</p><p>“God puts us in a position to be where we are,” he said. “I feel like it’ll be great for the city.”</p><p>Then his expression turned playful and he predicted:</p><p>“A lot of kids named Caleb in Chicago.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" </div> </div><p>We both chuckled, and I remembered that despite his 6-10 frame, his pursuit of GOAT status, his biblical namesake, he is still basically a teenager.</p><p>One who listens to 2000s Drake and goes for sad car rides down Lake Shore Drive. One who seems to genuinely enjoy the process of discovering himself and the world around him.</p><p>It made me miss my college years, when it was more acceptable to explore ideas just for the sake of exploring, so I asked him a question fit for that era. What did he think the equivalent of “bounce,” his defining trait, was for a quarterback?</p><p>He pondered it for a minute and tested out an answer: maybe it was a quarterback’s cadence at the line of scrimmage, or more generally, their swag.</p><p>Personally, I thought arm strength was the most logical comparison, but I appreciated that his answer was more creative. I left Bulls practice excited about the future of this unique and thoughtful 20-year old.</p><p>But I also felt reluctant for him to grow up and discover, as Williams already has, Chicago sports fandom in its fullness.</p><p>We are so willing to hope, to open our hearts to our young stars, and then, so quick to respond to disappointment or deviations from our expectations like betrayal. It can be tough, as Drake once put it, dealing with a heart that you didn’t break.</p><p>Even Williams, who in Year 3 has evolved into a MVP candidate leading a 7-2 Bears team, still deals with dramatic turns in public support, including fans calling him soft for “overreacting” to his hamstring injury earlier this season.</p><p>The silver lining for Wilson is he’s got someone in his corner who’s been through it before.</p><p>“If he needs any help … we’re building that friendship, that bond, that trust between each other,” Williams said of Wilson. “If he needs anything I’m always willing to help.</p><p>That help extends, of course, to pizza recommendations. Williams has already clued Wilson into Zarella Pizzeria in River North. (Like any self-respecting Chicagoans, Wilson and Williams enjoy deep dish but ultimately prefer tavern style). But the two have also traded words of encouragement about their injuries.</p><p>Wilson will now miss 4-6 weeks with his broken hand, the third hand injury he’s suffered this calendar year. Just another taste of the adversity that his parents saw coming.</p><p>Thank goodness he's got the Chicago Calebs Club keeping him company on the ride. </p>

entries.title: Connor Bedard injured in Blackhawks' wild victory against Maple Leafs
entries.summary: <p>Star center <b>Connor Bedard</b> suffered another injury while taking a faceoff during the Blackhawks’ 6-3 victory Tuesday against the Maple Leafs at the United Center.</p><p>Two minutes into the third period, Bedard was squaring off against Leafs center <b>Nick Paul </b>when Paul accidentally swiped Bedard’s right hand with his stick. Bedard immediately grimaced, fell and skated off to the locker room, slamming his stick and holding up his right arm.</p><p>Coach <b>Jeff Blashill </b>said later that Bedard will undergo further testing Wednesday.</p><p>‘‘It looked [like] what it looked like,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘I hate to comment further until I know more. Everybody saw it, so you can certainly draw your own conclusions. But I don’t know what that means, though.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This is the best replay of the Connor Bedard injury: <a href="https://t.co/5nDMy0ScE5">pic.twitter.com/5nDMy0ScE5</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2122884824767586645?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bedard injured his right shoulder on a faceoff last December against the Blues but recovered without surgery, missing 12 games. It’s far from certain that his injury Tuesday was to his shoulder.</p><p>He had surgery during the summer on his left shoulder after he crashed into the boards during an offseason training drill.</p><p>Before leaving the game, Bedard ripped off a perfectly placed snipe late in the second period, capping a crazy sequence that gave the Hawks (6-13-2) a 3-2 lead at the time. It was his 18th point in 15 games this season.</p><p>Even after he went down, the Hawks kept tacking on goals to pull away from the Leafs (8-13-2), who now have lost seven games in a row amid porous goaltending from pricey free-agent signee <b>Sergei Bobrovsky</b>.</p><p>‘‘When [Bedard is] in the lineup, he brings a certain amount of intensity that we all feed off of,’’ forward <b>Oliver Moore</b> said. ‘‘With a guy like him going down, it’s tough. He’s a huge piece for us. We had to make sure that we stayed on top of it. We wanted to do it for him a little bit.’’</p><p>Said Blashill: ‘‘ ‘Response’ was the word of the night. After they scored, we responded. After he got hurt, we responded.’’</p><h3>Still cooking</h3><p>Forward <b>Frank Nazar </b>scored twice to extend his hot streak. He now has three multigoal games in his last six and is up to 10 goals on the season.</p><p>Defenseman <b>Sam Rinzel</b> had three assists for his third consecutive multipoint game and now has 10 assists in his last eight games. Winger <b>Tyler Bertuzzi</b> added three points on two goals and an assist.</p><p>Blashill said he was pleased with how the Hawks defended the middle of the defensive zone and improved their breakouts.</p><p>‘‘Unfortunately, injuries are part of this thing, and we have to find a way to grind through them,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘At least they had some road map of how to grind through it after [Bedard] went out.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Tyler Bertuzzi taps in a nice feed from Rinzel on the power play. <a href="https://t.co/4kaovKmPEx">pic.twitter.com/4kaovKmPEx</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2122884965717446994?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Hall of Famers</b></h3><p>A sellout crowd of 19,988 filled the United Center as the Hawks celebrated the exact 100-year anniversary of their first game, which also was a victory against the Toronto franchise (then the St. Patricks).</p><p>The Hawks used the special night to announce the three 2027 inductees into their Hall of Fame. Based on fan, media and alumni ballots, former defenseman <b>Brent Seabrook </b>was inducted from the ‘‘Modern’’ category, former center <b>Jeremy Roenick</b> was inducted from the ‘‘Heritage’’ category and <b>Cliff Koroll</b> was inducted as a builder. Koroll spent his entire NHL career (1969-80) with the Hawks, totaling 462 points in 814 games before becoming an assistant coach. He also founded and served as president of the Hawks’ alumni association.</p><h3>Byram update</h3><p>Defenseman <b>Bowen Byram</b>, sidelined by a perplexing upper-body injury since Oct.  13, continues to practice with the team but already is ruled out for the Hawks’ game Thursday against the Blue Jackets.</p><p>Meanwhile, Byram’s wife, <b>Kailey</b>, announced Saturday on Instagram that the couple’s twin girls, born Oct. 3, are still in a neonatal intensive-care unit.</p>

entries.title: Illinois beats Duke 99-78 as Andrej Stojakovic scores record 46 points at Cameron Indoor
entries.summary: <p>DURHAM, N.C. — Andrej Stojakovic scored 46 points, the most ever by an opponent at Duke, to highlight a dominating performance from No. 10 Illinois in a 99-78 victory on Tuesday that ended the fifth-ranked Blue Devils' 35-game homecourt winning streak.</p><p>Stojakovic had 20 by halftime and finished 14 of 21 from the field and 16 of 20 from the foul line for the Fighting Illini (4-1), repeatedly beating any array of would-be defenders Duke sent his way. And by the end of the night, Stojakovic had posted the biggest scoring output by a visitor at Duke's famously rowdy Cameron Indoor Stadium, breaking the record of 43 points set by South Carolina's Grady Wallace in February 1957.</p><p>He came within two points of matching Duke's Dick Groat (48 in February 1952) for the most points by any player in Cameron's nearly 87-year history.</p><p>Freshman Quentin Coleman added 27 points as the Illini led 42-32 at the break and pushed that margin to 23 by midway through the second half.</p><p>Making it all the more impressive, the Illini — coming off the program's first Final Four trip in 21 years — stayed in firm control despite preseason Associated Press All-American David Mirkovic yet to play this season due to a foot injury and starter Jake Davis out since suffering an opening-night shoulder injury.</p><p>And the Illini didn't need a lights-out offensive show to do it — other than Stojakovic, anyway. They shot 43.1% and made just 6 of 32 3-pointers, but Illinois showed a physical edge by hammering Duke on the glass (54-34) and outscoring the Blue Devils 48-30 in the paint.</p><p>Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje had 17 points for Duke (3-2), which shot just 37.5% in suffering its first loss at Cameron since falling to rival North Carolina in March 2024 to close the regular season. It's the most lopsided home loss for Duke since March Madness expanded to 64 teams in 1985, surpassing a 20-point loss to UNC in 1989.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Illinois:</b> The Illini host Eastern Illinois on Friday.</p><p><b>Duke:</b> The Blue Devils face Washington State on Saturday in the Acrisure Series in Palm Desert, California.<br></p>

entries.title: Congress must deliver on Americans' affordability concerns
entries.summary: <p>Many Americans were surprised by the results of the midterm elections. The National Urban League and our nationwide network of affiliates were not.</p><p>For months, our affiliates, volunteers and partners were in neighborhoods across the country knocking on doors, staffing phone banks, registering voters and listening. What we heard was not partisan rhetoric. We heard anxiety. Parents worried about high grocery bills. Seniors stretched by rising housing costs and prescription expenses. Working families struggling to keep up with utility bills, childcare costs and the price of filling a gas tank. Young people wondering whether<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/03/trump-housing-counseling-funds-discrimination-affordability-marc-morial" > homeownership</a>, once a cornerstone of the American Dream, is now permanently out of reach.</p><p>Americans carried those concerns into the voting booth.</p><p>The results reshaped the political map. At least nine Senate seats and 40 House seats changed hands, with several races yet to be called. New voices emerged, and historic candidates triumphed.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Voters persisted through obstacles deliberately designed to discourage participation. Across the country, racially motivated gerrymandering, voter suppression laws, polling place closures and administrative barriers attempted to make civic participation more difficult. Yet voters showed up anyway. They made their voices heard. They demonstrated that democracy is strongest when every eligible voter can participate freely and fairly.</p><p>But the real measure of this moment is not who won. It is what the winners do next.</p><p>As I wrote in <a class="Link" href="https://nul.org/sites/default/files/2026-11/2026_CIV_MHM_Legislative_and_Oversight_Priorities_for_120th_Congress.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>a letter to congressional leaders</u></a>, the American people deserve a Congress that is responsive to their everyday challenges, safeguards their fundamental rights and exercises its constitutional responsibilities with independence and integrity. For working families, the measure of congressional success will be whether wages keep pace with costs, housing becomes more affordable, essential services remain accessible and economic opportunity expands.</p><p>The National Urban League has a name for this vision: <a class="Link" href="https://nul.org/sites/default/files/2026-09/2026_FINAL%20Affordability%20for%20All%20Memo%20%28External%20Use%29.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Affordability for All</u></a>.</p><p>Our Affordability for All agenda recognizes a simple truth. The affordability crisis is not limited to one expense or one demographic group. It is interconnected. Housing costs affect family wealth. Healthcare costs affect financial stability. Education costs affect future earnings. Transportation costs affect access to opportunity. When families are squeezed from every direction, prosperity becomes impossible.</p><p>The agenda’s five interconnected policy priorities represent a comprehensive framework for strengthening economic security, expanding opportunity and ensuring that economic growth benefits working families:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-e0e8a021-e2d1-11f1-a527-912e534f9770" start="1"><li>A national minimum wage that reflects the actual cost of living and automatically adjusts to inflation, preventing future erosion of workers' purchasing power</li><li>The repeal of the "Big Ugly Bill" (One Big Beautiful Bill) and restoration of essential investments in working families such as Medicaid, Affordable Care Act coverage, nutrition assistance programs, federal student aid, workforce development and other critical supports</li><li>A comprehensive federal housing policy that addresses both the supply of affordable housing and the ability of families to afford available homes, including expansion of the Section 8 housing choice voucher program, adequate funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development and its core housing programs</li><li>Affordable broadband access and promotion of an inclusive digital economy through restoration of the Affordable Connectivity Program and other policies that provide affordable access to both broadband service and the devices necessary to participate in the digital economy</li><li>An end to inflationary tariffs that increase costs for American families and trade policies that support American competitiveness and domestic economic growth without imposing additional financial burdens on families already struggling with the cost of living</li></ol><p>As policymakers debate these priorities, they should remember the message voters delivered this year. People are tired of being told the economy is strong while their own finances feel fragile. They are tired of hearing statistics that fail to reflect their own lived experience. They want leaders who understand that affordability is not merely an economic issue. It is a quality-of-life issue. It is a family issue. It is a democracy issue.</p><p>When working people cannot afford housing, healthcare, food, transportation, or education, faith in institutions begins to erode. When families can build wealth, own homes, educate their children and retire with dignity, democracy becomes stronger.</p><p>The National Urban League will continue working with our affiliates, partners and supporters to ensure that voters remain informed and engaged. Through our <a class="Link" href="https://nul.org/washington-bureau" target="_blank" >Washington Bureau</a> and our Affordability for All agenda, we will continue advocating for policies that lower costs, expand opportunity and strengthen economic mobility for every American.</p><p>The voters have done their part. They organized. They voted. They made their voices heard.</p><p>Now it is time for Congress to do theirs.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1c0000" name="module-1c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Married man has four kids with the 'other woman'
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I was in a relationship with a married man for more than 20 years. A year ago, I found out he was cheating on me, so I ended the relationship. We have four children under the age of 18, and our relationship has caused them nothing but heartache because he chose his wife over them.</p><p>I was so blinded by having the family I yearned for that I didn't see how toxic the relationship was to everyone. I'm working toward building a better relationship with my children, but I think it's hard for them to trust me because of my previous refusal to end my involvement with him. Do you have any suggestions besides time to bring us closer? — <i>BLINDED BY HIM IN THE NORTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR BLINDED:</b> Did you really tell your children that your lover had chosen his wife over them? If you did, it was heartless. They had nothing to do with his unwillingness to commit to you, and for the sake of their self-esteem you should make that clear.</p><p>Family counseling might help bring you closer to your children. It may also help you come to terms with the fact that you wasted so many years on this man — and understand why you did it — so you can move on. If you can manage that, there's hope that they can, too.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We recently did a favor for a young couple who work for us. We were happy to do it and did not expect or want any type of repayment. They decided to thank us with a nice gift of tickets to an event that takes place on a day when we are unavailable. In addition, it is three hours away from us, and, due to my mobility issues, we cannot take a long trip in the car. It's also not something we would normally be interested in.</p><p>It seems strange and random that someone would give us such a gift, not knowing if we're available, interested or able. I graciously thanked them for the gift and told them that we're not going to be able to use it and why. I suggested that they try to give it to somebody else who can use the tickets. They were not cheap! I'm feeling bad now for rejecting the gift. But if we had accepted it and pretended we were going to like and use it, it would have been a lie. Did I do the right thing? — <i>RETHINKING REJECTION</i></p><p><b>DEAR RETHINKING:</b> When you receive a material gift in a reasonable price range, it's usually best to accept it politely and not explain why you can't or won't use it. However, because these were pricey tickets to an event, and accepting would have deprived someone else of the ability to attend, you did exactly the right thing. The key is to be prompt and polite in your refusal, which you were. Imagine the awkwardness if you had lied and they later asked whether you had enjoyed yourselves at the event!</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: No to Rubio
entries.summary: <p>You hear the hopeful sighs among certain Republicans looking to move past Donald Trump and seeing JD Vance mired in quicksand. <i>Maybe Rubio could be the future? He has MAGA credibility but without the cutthroat affect of JD or DeSantis. He was confirmed 99-0 in the Senate. He's Hispanic. He's clearly not full MAGA</i>.</p><p>Forget it. I say this as someone who would dearly love to see the GOP turn away from Trump and MAGA. But Marco Rubio is not the vehicle. He may not have personally bitten the heads off the chickens, but he enjoyed the meal.</p><p>Let's consider the ways in which he has permanently stained his character. And for the sake of space as well as mercy, let's limit our scope just to Trump's second term.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-010000" name="module-010000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Rubio tamely accepted Trump 2.0's mortifying initial executive orders, including the one Trump signed the day before Rubio took office purporting to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America." Anyone with a modicum of character would have contradicted his boss and risked the consequences. Trump would probably have taken it well, since it was early in the term and firing his secretary of state over such a matter would have been a bad look, even for him. He might have joked, <i>Marco doesn't like it. He must love Mexico.</i> But leaving aside Trump's likely reaction, Rubio had the opportunity to do the right thing but let it pass.</p><p>While serving as secretary of state, Rubio also accepted the job as head of the National Archives after Trump summarily fired Colleen Shogan. Her offense was to head up the office that had reported to the Justice Department that Trump had absconded with classified documents when leaving office in 2021 and repeatedly refused to return them. By taking the job, Rubio ratified Trump's corrupt termination of Shogan (who wasn't even in charge when the National Archives turned Trump in), as well as his violation of the Espionage Act.</p><p>After Signalgate, Rubio accepted the additional job of national security advisor, thus tacitly approving the influence of Laura Loomer, who had gotten most of Mike Waltz's staff fired and may have played a role in Waltz's sacking, too. He also ratified the scapegoating of Waltz for Signalgate, and while the former advisor deserved blame, he deserved it no more than Pete Hegseth, Tulsi Gabbard and others of the president's closest allies and confidants, including Rubio himself. Again, Rubio could have done the right thing but let it pass.</p><p>When Elon Musk and his pimple-faced enforcers stormed into U.S. Agency for International Development to pull funding from immunization programs, close down rural African clinics and cancel food aid to hundreds of thousands of the neediest people on the planet (all in violation of the law), Rubio could have protested. Hell, by then he was head of USAID, too. When Musk tweeted that USAID was a "criminal organization" and that it was "time for it to die," Rubio mumbled some lame words: "There are things that USAID, that we do through USAID, that we should continue to do, and we will continue to do. This is not about ending the programs that USAID does, per se." Not per se, but per fact. Say it with me: Rubio could have done the right thing but let it pass.</p><p>The secretary of state is considered <i>the</i> premier cabinet post: The secretary is the nation's chief diplomat, is fourth in the presidential succession and is often the president's chief foreign policy advisor. Rubio, as both secretary of state and national security advisor, ought to dominate this administration's foreign policy as no single advisor has since Henry Kissinger. But Rubio could not dissuade Trump from threatening to invade the territory of one of our closest allies, nor from menacing Canada, Mexico, Cuba, Panama and Colombia. Rubio was effectively by Trump's side on "Liberation Day," when Trump declared a trade war on the entire world and was an active participant in the decision to invade and plunder Venezuela. In fact, it was Rubio who strutted and boasted after the fact, "Don't play games with this president when he's in office, because it's not going to turn out well." What must have been going through his mind when Trump announced, at a post-Nicolas-Maduro-snatch press conference, that Rubio would henceforth be running Venezuela? It must have been unprintable. Rubio could have done the right thing ...</p><p>In the last two years, the U.S. military has conducted something like 68 extrajudicial strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Pacific and Caribbean — including on vessels that were not suspected of carrying drugs or weapons — resulting in about 230 fatalities. At least some of those deaths were "double tap" strikes of people clinging to wreckage, which violates the Geneva Conventions and our own laws. It's premeditated murder. Previous secretaries of state have resigned on principle for far less. Rubio could have done ...</p><p>Rubio may have wished to disappear into the sofa cushions when Trump and Vance humiliated Volodymyr Zelensky in an Oval Office beatdown that should live in infamy, but he failed to defend our beleaguered ally and instead piled on, saying later that Zelensky needed to apologize.</p><p>He failed to prevent Trump from undertaking a war on Iran that was the most impulsive, least well-considered act of the dumbest president in history.<br>Well, you may say, it's not Rubio's fault that he worked for such a fool. But yes, it very much is. And by so doing he has forfeited the right to be considered for any future role in American government.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-560000" name="module-560000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Black Chicagoans feel joy of Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
entries.summary: <p>My most-told story about how my grandma migrated to Chicago from Greenwood, Mississippi, in 1940 is what happened when she got here. At just 17 years old, she boarded a train to a city — and climate — she didn’t know. She hadn’t packed a coat and learned firsthand why the Windy City got its moniker when she stepped on that platform and the cold and chill of the Chicago spring immediately hit her.</p><p>But while she wasn’t quite prepared for Chicago, Chicago was prepared for <i>her</i>. Her cousin arrived at the train station to pick up the stubborn teen and welcome her with a nice warm coat. Soon, she’d learn, this city wasn’t so different from the one she was running away from. And, like the oft-repeated quote from Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners” so aptly reminds us today: “Chicago ain’t nothing but Mississippi with tall buildings.”</p><p>That’s because Chicago couldn’t be Chicago <i>without</i> Mississippi. During the Great Migration, more Black people came to Chicago from Mississippi than from any other state. My grandma and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wttw.com/dusable-to-obama/the-great-migration" target="_blank" >half-million</a> others are why the tie between the state and this city is so strong. It’s also why Black Chicagoans are feeling a particular connection to the joy our Southern families are feeling now that Mississippi has its first Black senator since Reconstruction.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f40000" name="module-f40000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Here in Chicago, I’ve seen a celebration for our Mississippi family: people doing shout-outs about where they’re from, telling family stories, even steppin’ in celebration.</p><p>Over a third of Mississippi’s residents are Black, the highest percentage of any state. And yet, it took 145 years for Sen.-elect Scott Colom to be elected to represent it. And Black Mississippians fought for this victory. Voter drives and organizing against suppression worked, and according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6038701/midterm-election-voter-turnout-south" target="_blank" ><u>NPR election result data</u></a>, Mississippi was among the states in which majority-Black counties had high voter turnout.</p><p>A century and a half is a long time to be without representation, and I think about this timeline in the perspective of my own family. Between 1881 and today, my family had four generations of Black Mississippians and only two generations born in Chicago. For Black people like me, it’s impossible not to feel an immense sense of pride.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8a0000" name="image-8a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/be94ac7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fa7dc00/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6600278/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A black and white photo shows a woman holding a small child. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6600278/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/48b8449/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6600278/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3024x1697+0+1167/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F59%2F31%2F26edaca241efa9a645e85a27d4a9%2Fimg-3632.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The author’s grandmother, Bertha Eatmon, holding her daughter Janice, the author’s aunt, in Bronzeville in 1954. Eatmon arrived in Chicago from Mississippi when she was 17.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Tanikia “Nikki” Carpenter told me she feels the same way. Her family is mostly from Sunflower County, where my dad’s side of the family is from.</p><p>“We have a saying in our family that we're Mississippi mud, and that means we can't forget where we came from,” she told me. “That's our roots.”</p><p>A writer who lives on the South Side, Carpenter wrote a play titled <a class="Link" href="https://americanwritersmuseum.org/program-calendar/emmetts-photo-a-live-reading/" target="_blank" >“Emmett’s Photo”</a> that reimagines the moments before photos of Black Chicago teen Emmett Till, who was killed visiting family in Mississippi, were published in <a class="Link" href="https://www.loc.gov/collections/civil-rights-history-project/articles-and-essays/murder-of-emmett-till/" target="_blank" >JET magazine</a> in 1955 — an action that helped galvanize the Civil Rights Movement.</p><p>Like Carpenter's relatives, some elders in my family experienced trauma from their years in Mississippi, which meant they couldn’t always talk about what they’d been through there. Some struggled to return or to even mention what they’d witnessed. It’s a strange, foggy gap in knowledge that newer generations like mine are trying to fill in with hopeful trips to Mississippi and searches for connection.</p><h3>Mississippi’s moxie</h3><p>While our elders’ pain and fear from the past sometimes created a physical division for us, we are seeing what might be a new era for Black Mississippi as an opportunity for us to support and recommit ourselves to our ancestral land. There’s an energy that reminds people of something Colom said on the campaign trail: Mississippi matters.</p><p>Carpenter feels like this is a positive step.</p><p>“It feels like it's going in the right direction; it feels like even if no one comes to help Mississippi, they are down there helping themselves,” she said, adding that Mississippi is one of the most misunderstood places in America. “And so I'm so excited for them, and I'm ready to go back and just be with my people, explore even more of my roots.”</p><p>During his <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C7jOeSZbozU" target="_blank" >victory speech</a> at the historic Tougaloo College, Colom mentioned how U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., and NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson — whom he calls his mentors — warned him: “We don't think the cavalry is coming.”</p><p>Black voters in Mississippi became that cavalry.</p><p>"Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out,” Johnson said in a statement, adding that this win happened in “a state that has witnessed some of the nation's most difficult battles for voting rights.”</p><p>But like when my grandma finally got that winter coat, things are looking up.</p><p><i>Arionne Nettles is a news editor at Chicago Public Media, where she edits cross-platform work across digital, print and audio at WBEZ and the Sun-Times</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-640000" name="module-640000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Chicago man cleared in Gregory Bovino murder plot fights deportation to stay with family
entries.summary: <p>Ten months<b> </b>have passed<b> </b>since<b> </b>Juan<b> </b>Espinoza<b> </b>Martinez<b> </b>heard the words “not guilty”<b> </b>— but he’s still not a free man.</p><p>Immigration authorities have held<b> </b>the<b> </b>Little<b> </b>Village<b> </b>resident<b> </b>in custody<b> </b>since<b> </b>he was acquitted of plotting<b> </b>the<b> </b>murder<b> </b>of<b> </b>then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino,<b> </b>the controversial face of the Trump administration’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/08/trump-chicago-crime-pritzker-national-guard-ice-truth-social" >audacious Midway Blitz deportation campaign</a> in the Chicago area.</p><p>In a call arranged by his legal team<b> </b>this week, Espinoza Martinez said<b> </b>he’d rather sit behind bars<b> </b>than be deported to a country<b> </b>he doesn’t remember<b> </b>— without his loved ones.</p><p>“I’m not abandoning my family,” Espinoza Martinez told the Chicago Sun-Times. “I’m going to try as hard as I can. I’m going to hold on, incarcerated, because I’m not giving up.”</p><p>His fight for freedom has now stretched more than a year, starting<b> </b>when<b> </b>federal authorities <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/06/feds-say-ranking-latin-king-offered-10k-for-bovinos-murder" >accused<b> </b>him<b> </b>of<b> </b>soliciting<b> </b>Bovino’s<b> </b>murder</a>.</p><p>Espinoza Martinez put his fate in the hands of a jury, in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/19/chicagos-first-midway-blitz-trial-could-revolve-around-the-feds-bovino-murder-for-hire-claim" >only trial to result from Operation Midway Blitz</a>. The panel<b> </b>swiftly<b> </b>acquitted<b> </b>him<b> </b>in January, deliberating only<b> </b>about<b> </b>three hours.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4d0000" name="image-4d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0e3fdd7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2528x1419+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F42%2F2ae3e9074918aa325edceeaa0449%2Fbovinohearing-102925-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f299fe4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2528x1419+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F42%2F2ae3e9074918aa325edceeaa0449%2Fbovinohearing-102925-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0ddf808/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2528x1419+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F42%2F2ae3e9074918aa325edceeaa0449%2Fbovinohearing-102925-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino leaves the Dirksen Federal Courthouse after testifying about immigration enforcement in Chicago in October 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Espinoza Martinez knew that wouldn’t be the end of the story.</p><p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/24/juan-espinoza-martinez-bovino-murder-plot-ice-custody" >took him into custody</a><b> </b>the next day. And he’s now being held in the Greene<b> </b>County<b> </b>Jail<b> </b>in Missouri, ICE records show.</p><p>ICE wouldn’t comment when contacted Tuesday.<b> </b>Homeland Security didn’t respond.</p><p>Espinoza Martinez, 38, said he was brought to the United States as a small child. A judge described him as a Mexican<b> </b>citizen<b> </b>who<b> </b>entered<b> </b>the<b> </b>United States<b> </b>as a minor, over 30 years ago,<b> </b>“without inspection or lawful admission.”</p><p>His case is another striking example of the damage done when prosecutors level high-profile charges that don’t hold up in court.</p><p>Not only did the feds accuse Espinoza Martinez of the murder plot,<b> </b>court records identified him as a “ranking member of the Latin Kings.”<b> </b>Espinoza Martinez’s criminal defense attorneys, Jonathan<b> </b>Bedi<b> </b>and<b> </b>Dena<b> </b>Singer, denied<b> </b>he had any gang affiliation<b> </b>or criminal history.</p><p>Bedi said their client “consistently worked to provide for his family while contributing positively to the community” — and even coached his kids’ sports teams.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/07/feds-wont-try-to-prove-gang-membership-for-man-charged-with-putting-a-bounty-on-greg-bovino" >Prosecutors eventually backed down</a><b> </b>from their claim<b> </b>about the Latin Kings.<b> </b>That<b> </b>prompted<b> </b>a judge to<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/15/federal-judge-bars-gang-evidence-from-bovino-murder-for-hire-trial" >bar<b> </b>gang-related testimony</a><b> </b>from the trial. And a week later, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" >the jury<b> </b>found<b> </b>Espinoza<b> </b>Martinez<b> </b>not guilty</a><b> </b>in one of several Midway Blitz prosecutions that collapsed at Chicago’s Dirksen Federal Courthouse.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: In CPS win, Jessica Biggs’ took precincts across the city but her coattails were not long, data shows
entries.summary: <p>Chicago chose its first fully elected school board on Nov. 3, with voters picking the Chicago Teachers Union-backed candidates for 10 of 20 board seats, with one still close to call, and for president, Jessica Biggs, with the support of anti-CTU forces.</p><p>After expensive campaigns where voters were pummeled with mailers, digital ads and, for the president’s race, incessant negative commercials, a Sun-Times and WBEZ analysis of Chicago Board of Election voter data shows how the winning candidates managed to rack up the votes.</p><p>Biggs, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" ><u>who won with 49% of the vote</u></a>, did best in majority white areas where fewer families send their children to public school. But she also outdid her two opponents in predominately Black areas, though she didn’t get a majority of votes.</p><p>Despite her decisive win, Biggs’ dominance in some voting precincts did not rub off on school board candidates that were also supported by political groups that opposed the teachers union, the analysis shows.</p><p>Keep reading to learn more about what the voter data says about where candidates came up short, where winners got their support, and what the data says about their mandate.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-2f0000" name="html-embed-module-2f0000"></a><figure class="elex-map-embed"> <h3 class="elex-map-title">Chicago school board president results by precinct</h3> <iframe src="https://kcinbk.github.io/chicago_election2026/" title="Map of Chicago school board president election results by precinct" loading="lazy"> </iframe> <figcaption class="elex-map-credit"> <span><b>Source:</b> <a href="https://chicagoelections.gov" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Chicago Board of Election Commissioners</a></span> <span><b>Graphic and analysis:</b> Keenan Chen/Chicago Sun-Times</span> </figcaption> </figure> <style> .elex-map-embed { width: 100%; max-width: 1000px; margin: 24px auto; padding: 0; } .elex-map-title { font-family: var(--font-2) !important; font-size: 26px !important; line-height: 1.15; letter-spacing: 0; color: #000; margin: 0 0 16px; padding: 0; } .elex-map-embed iframe { display: block; width: 100%; height: 650px; border: 0; } .elex-map-credit { font-family: "Proxima Nova", sans-serif; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.6; color: #000; margin: 16px 0 0; padding: 0; } .elex-map-credit span { display: block; } .elex-map-credit b { font-weight: 700; } .elex-map-credit a { color: #000; text-decoration: underline; } @media (max-width: 600px) { .elex-map-title { font-size: 22px; } .elex-map-embed iframe { height: 520px; } } </style> </div> </div><p>By Election Day, three of five of the original candidates were still in the running for school board president. Jessica Biggs, an incumbent and former Chicago Public Schools principal, beat out Hilario Dominguez, CTU’s former deputy political director, and prominent defense attorney Victor Henderson. Sendhil Revuluri withdrew from the race after ballots had already been printed.</p><p>About 86% of the more than 790,000 Chicagoans who voted this fall cast a ballot in the school board president's race. That’s a little shy of the 94% who voted for Cook County Board president. About 83% participated in the school board district races, including five uncontested contests.</p><p>Biggs’ main pitch was that she is a consensus builder who could cut through conflicts and move an agenda forward. She also said she would bring together city and state leaders to create a financial stability plan for the district that includes showing “that CPS can spend responsibly before asking them to invest more.”</p><p>During and after the campaign, Biggs boasted about her broad coalition of support that included the union that represents CPS support staff, as well as several former city and school district leaders who worked under former Mayor Rahm Emanuel. She also took $1 million from billionaire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>Michael Sacks,</u></a> who advised Emanuel.</p><p>Biggs was helped by the fact that an anti-CTU political group called Common Ground Collective spent more than $3.5 million million to oppose Dominguez. That group, along with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, a centrist pro-school choice group, were united in an effort to wrest control of the school board from the CTU. Union-backed candidates, which, by virtue of having a former CTU organizer elected mayor, held the majority of the mayoral-appointed seats for the past two years in addition to winning several elected seats in 2024.</p><p>Biggs did particularly well on the North and Far Northwest sides, where voter turnout was high and people voted overwhelmingly for Biggs.</p><p>In these areas, which include the wealthy Lincoln Park area and more grassroot liberal areas in Rogers Park, Biggs got more votes than both her opponents combined.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-920000" name="html-embed-module-920000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30901069"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30901069/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Biggs, who said she wasn’t going to raise property taxes to the limit — the one measure the board currently has to increase revenue — performed at her peak in majority White areas where fewer families send their children to public schools, voter data shows.</p><p>But in parts of the South Side, West Side and majority Latino neighborhoods on the Northwest Side, Dominguez and Henderson combined got more votes than Biggs. Dominguez, who is Latino, alone got almost half of all votes in majority Latino neighborhoods.</p><p>Yet Henderson, who is Black, did not dominate in predominantly Black areas. He only got about 30% of the votes in these areas, compared to 47% for Biggs, who is white, and 21% for Dominguez.</p><p>Black voters may have favored Biggs because, as a former teacher and principal who was serving on the board, had the most experience in the education system, said Rufus Williams, a former school board president under Mayor Richard M. Daley and a host on WVON, a radio station that caters to Chicago’s Black community.</p><p>Williams said he thinks some Black voters were wary of Dominguez’ close relationship with the CTU, especially because of the role the board president will have in negotiating a contract with the union.</p><p>Also, Biggs had the money to get her name out there. Williams notes that Che “Rhymefest” Smith, a Hip-Hop artist who is Black and ran unopposed in the district that includes Woodlawn and Hyde Park, was featured in commercials on WVON touting Biggs.</p><p>“I think those things matter,” Williams said.</p><p>But CTU President Stacy Davis Gates attributed Biggs’ win to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" >big money that flooded TV</a> with negative ads about Dominguez. These ads focused on half truths about unsubstantiated allegations and whether taxes were paid on a family property.</p><p>“They put on the table a million dollars not to debate whether or not the rich should pay their fair share, not to debate whether or not Black children deserve a fully funded school with libraries,” Gates said on election night. “They spent a million dollars a week to try and lie on people. They cannot win the argument, which is why they didn't have the argument.”</p><p>Jackson Potter, vice president of the CTU, adds that Biggs’ messaging was “strategically ambiguous,” as she seemed to get behind some of the ideas promoted by CTU, such as quality neighborhood schools and an expansion of early childhood education. Only when pressed, he argued, did Biggs talk about how she was open to closing schools or fiscal responsibility, which can translate into cutting staff.</p><p>He also said some of the heavy focus on defeating Dominguez might have resulted in CTU candidates on the district level having an easier time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><div class="cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper"> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/30936782"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30936782/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> <div class="cpm-gfx-embed"> <div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/30937302"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30937302/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div> <figcaption class="elex-map-credit"> <span><b>Notes:</b> "No CTU and anti-CTU match-up" refers to a race where a candidate ran unopposed or where only one camp (CTU or anti-CTU) backed a candidate. District 10a had a CTU-backed candidate but she was a write-in and was not on the ballot. Write-in candidate totals have not been fully released.</span> <br> <span><b>Graphic and analysis:</b> Keenan Chen/Chicago Sun-Times</span> </figcaption> </figure> <style> .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: start; display: flex; flex-direction: row; gap: 2rem; } .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper .cpm-gfx-embed { flex: 1; min-width: 18rem; } @media screen and (max-width: 30rem) { .cpm-gfx-2up-embeds-wrapper { align-items: stretch; flex-direction: column; gap: 0; } } </style> </div> </div><p>In some areas, Biggs dominance in the president’s race did not translate into school board candidates backed by the same anti-CTU interests also doing well. In the 10 school board districts where Biggs was the top vote-getter, six candidates supported by the teachers union or the political group that funded it, Our Schools, were victorious. The candidate supported by anti-CTU forces only won four times.</p><p>The CTU/Our Schools candidates dubbed themselves “public school champions” and pledged not to close schools and instead demand that the state come through with more money to fund schools. They also supported broader ideas, including expanding universal pre-school to three-year-olds.</p><p>The CTU and Our Schools <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" target="_blank" ><u>spent significantly less money</u></a> than Common Ground Collective and the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. Those are the two major spenders in the anti-CTU camp. Common Ground Collective and The Urban Center made official endorsements in district races. While they did not endorse in the president’s race, the super PACs connected to Common Ground Collective and INCS spent money attacking Dominguez.</p><p>Despite being outspent, the CTU-endorsed candidates were able to capture half of the 20 school board district seats, with one additional seat <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-district-6a-results" target="_blank" ><u>still too close to call</u></a>. Their candidates did particularly well in Latino areas and in areas with more than 75% of children enrolled in public schools, voter data shows.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6f0000" name="html-embed-module-6f0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30902837"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30902837/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Six races were not included in the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis because those contests didn’t feature a CTU-backed candidate against an anti-CTU candidate.</p><p>The anti-CTU forces claimed all of those school board seats, including five that were uncontested, giving their numbers a big lift<b>. </b></p><p>In three school districts, two incumbents and one newcomer were kicked off the ballot through petition challenges. The Urban Center, one of the anti-CTU groups, hired lawyers to successfully pursue those challenges.</p><p>And in other two districts, only the incumbent board members, both of whom typically vote with the anti-CTU block, filed petitions to get on the ballot. Both were ultimately re-elected.</p><p>The anti-CTU forces argue that the fact that CTU didn’t run candidates in these races was a failure on the union’s part, with the executive director of Common Ground Collective writing in Crain’s Chicago Business that “the vaunted CTU political operation stunningly stumbled out of the gate.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Chicago School Board election results</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-99ebbb22-d88c-11f1-a0f8-2966deb425a8"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-results" target="_blank" >What you need to know about all 21 races</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/06/chicago-school-board-ctu-teachers-union-spending" target="_blank" >Political groups spent $12 million to defeat CTU candidates. One losing race cost $76 per vote.</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" target="_blank" >CTU poised to capture half of school board district seats, but loses president’s race</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" target="_blank" >Jessica Biggs wins president race</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago animal rights activist is sentenced to jail time after falsely reporting shooting at 'backyard rodeo'
entries.summary: <p>A longtime animal rights activist in Chicago was sentenced to 60 days in jail, 60 hours of community service and a year of probation after being found guilty of hounding dispatchers downstate and making a false report of a shooting with the aim of getting police sent to a “backyard rodeo” where she believes livestock were being mistreated.</p><p>North Side resident Jodie Wiederkehr, 57, was sentenced this month by Ogle County Judge Anthony Peska after a jury found her guilty of a felony and a misdemeanor. With "day-for-day" good-behavior credit, the 60-day sentence would translate into 30 days.</p><p>Backyard rodeos have been held in rural and semi-rural locales in Illinois in recent years, including some suburban sites.</p><p>The rodeos often include an event called “steer tailing,” which involves someone on horseback chasing down a fleeing steer and wrapping a leg around the animal’s tail, with the intent of it tumbling to the ground. Beyond injuries from the fall, the steers sometimes have their tails ripped free in the process, something called “degloving.”</p><p>Animal rights activists have been trying to halt the practice, arguing it violates the state’s animal cruelty statute, though some say the wording is too vague to prosecute under. There have been unsuccessful legislative efforts to refine the law to more explicitly bar steer tailing statewide, while some county governments are also taking it on.</p><p>Wiederkehr — a member of SHARK, which stands for SHowing Animals Respect and Kindness — said she was remotely monitoring one of the rodeos being held last year in the Rochelle area west of DeKalb, “getting the play-by-play from the field team that was there” monitoring the event via drone.</p><p>“There were steers being degloved, overworked, criminally abused,” she said.</p><p>She said she called the Ogle County sheriff’s non-emergency number numerous times and, frustrated and angry that nobody was going to be sent, ultimately told a dispatcher there was a shooting in an attempt to force a police response.</p><p>There had been no shooting, and Wiederkehr said she regrets saying that, and is embarrassed, but in the moment was “distraught.”</p><p>“Two steers and a horse got legs broken at a previous rodeo there,” she said.</p><p>She insisted she “didn’t harass” the dispatchers, saying that “each time I called there was a crime happening” that amounted to animal cruelty, but wasn’t taken seriously.</p><p>Her attorneys asked for no jail time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" from a legitimate emergency.</p><p>Wiederkehr argued that, while she made a mistake, the sheriff’s office did not really believe there’d been a shooting, and that she was prosecuted because Ogle County State’s Attorney Mike Rock was angry about Wiederkehr previously criticizing him over a lack of prosecutions involving the rodeos.</p><p>Wiederkehr’s lawyers filed court papers portraying this allowed a prison sentence on the felony of up to three years.</p><p>Chris Carraway, one of Wiederkehr’s attorneys, said Peska previously has gone lighter on more serious offenses, including an incident in which a teenager threatened to "shoot up" a school and got 24 months of probation.</p><p>Peska wouldn’t let Wiederkehr present a defense based on the argument “that I broke the law to prevent a greater harm,” she said. Nor would the judge let the jury see video of the rodeo in which animals were mistreated, Carraway said.</p><p>Rock said “they wanted to turn this into a week-long trial of whether steer tailing is appropriate or not when the issue was whether she made repeated calls and ultimately a false report of a criminal offense.”</p><p>An appeal on the sentence, conviction or both is expected.</p><p>Under pressure, organizers of the Ogle County rodeo have stopped holding the event.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/05/suburban-backyard-rodeos-steer-tailing-animal-cruelty" target="_blank" >Suburban backyard rodeos under fire, with steers knocked down, sometimes stripped of their tails</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/mchenry-county-judge-acquits-backyard-rodeo-steer-woodstock" target="_blank" >Man who kicked a steer in its head at suburban backyard rodeo acquitted on animal cruelty charge</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
