entries.title: Review: Chicago Shakes’ ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’
entries.summary: <p>In October, Chicago Shakespeare Theatre opened its production of “The Winter’s Tale,” and now, running in repertory with that high-quality but uneven production, we have an even better, intensely physical, quite rip-roaring “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” with the same director (the theater’s leader Edward Hall), elegantly bare set (from designer Michael Pavelka), and cast, along with an extremely similar opening framing device.</p><p>This isn’t exactly a traditional repertory approach familiar to Shakespearean companies in England and elsewhere (the Oregon and Stratford Shakespeare Festivals, for example). Those generally involve engaging an ensemble for an entire season of plays, but the productions themselves don’t necessarily have direct relationships to each other beyond sharing casts.</p><p>These two shows, though, weren’t just cast together but clearly conceptualized simultaneously. They come across as fraternal twins offering a unifying take on Shakespeare as a creator of fantasy.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Jan. 3<br><b>Where:</b> Chicago Shakespeare Theater, 800 E. Grand Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $65-$125<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoshakes.com/" target="_blank" >chicagoshakes.com</a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hour and 20 minutes with one intermission</div> </div><p>Hall begins both productions with a bed and a character reading a children’s book, which emphasizes innocence, playfulness and imagination. It’s not the seasonal references of the titles — “Winter” and “Midsummer” — that jump out with this choice, but the storytelling qualities of “Tale” and “Dream.”</p><p>In “Midsummer,” the storybook is presented by the impish Puck, played with proper joyous mischievousness by Patty Roache. Roache also sets the physical bar for the show by performing impressive gymnastic moves on hanging ribbons for Puck’s first monologue, an emblem of the magical nature of the fairy world, led by the elaborately garbed Oberon (Sean Fortunato) and Titania (Jessica Dean Turner). The servant fairies pop through a surprising number of trapdoors, dressed in ruffled white collars, pointed clown hats and masks, like figures out of <i>commedia dell’arte</i>.</p><p>The Oberon-Titania scenes here have a certain emotional restraint, but that certainly isn’t true of the core lover scenes. From their first entrance, the four romantic leads bound about with chaotic energy to match the nature of their oversized and inconstant emotions. Lysander (Dan Haller) and Demetrius (Esteban Ortiz-Villacorta) are both over the moon for Hermia (Felicia Oduh), and then for her oft-self-deprecating friend Helena (Grace Steckler), all thanks to Puck’s anarchic interventions.</p><p>Once the confusion begins, it’s all intense fun, with two special contributions particularly worth mentioning: Steckler provides the sincerity that also makes us care about how it ends, and fight and intimacy choreographer Zev Steinrock enables these talented young actors to throw themselves at and onto each other with an extremely effective sense of abandon. That’s difficult, and rare. And very funny. I was certainly surprised by the level of physicality that continued even when the actors entered the audience.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Dressed in Edwardian music-hall tweeds, these players are led by two ensemble members who stand out across both shows. Chiké Johnson lends an inner touch of noble confidence from his kingly character in “The Winter’s Tale,” and adds a perpetual smile to the big-egoed and much-abused Bottom here, making him as endearing as he is ridiculous. And Erik Hellman, as Quince, shows us (again!) how subtle excellent acting can be, and how simple, sharp lucidity can make supporting characters feel essential. In a show that’s an enviable embarrassment of comic riches, Hellman provides perhaps the most ideal, meta moment of all in the very meta “Midsummer” when he experiences a momentary actor’s nightmare once the spotlight hits.</p><p>On occasion, I thought the show sacrificed too much human vulnerability for performative preening, particularly with the lovers. But it requires a lot of careful self-control to make a show feel this physically urgent, and the overripe qualities of the lovers ended up coming across as purposeful. At the end we’re watching them, whom we’ve been laughing at for their oversized absurdity, make fun of the mechanicals’ oversized absurdity. That element — their condescension as an obvious show of self-blindness — works here in a way I haven’t seen before. This is certainly a superior production of one of Shakespeare’s most delightful plays.</p><p>In the end, the artist whose work most shines through the combination of productions is not an actor at all, but Pavelka, whose costume designs have a notable continuity — the refined use of black and white, the pops of rock-star leather and glamour contrasted with threads of nostalgia. Within all the eclecticism, there’s clarity, a clear reference to multiple performance traditions and on occasion, assisted by Marcus Doshi’s lighting, an extravagant beauty that’s quite extraordinary.</p><p>It’s the design work in these shows that connects them into a single, Shakespearean fantasy.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Chicago’s Japanese garden has a long history that almost disappeared
entries.summary: <p>This summer, after visiting the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park, I walked over to the Osaka Garden across the street. It was my first time seeing the tranquil garden and its manicured paths, small wooden bridge and fish pond. I had learned about it last year after writing a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/08/02/world-war-ii-america-japan-nuclear-war-hiroshima-nagasaki-amy-yee" target="_blank" ><u>column</u></a> about the 80th anniversary of the nuclear bombings in Japan.</p><p>One Curious City listener wanted to know if the garden was around during the 1893 World’s Fair.</p><p>It turns out its origins do date back to the Columbian Exposition, and the garden has lived several lives. It was burned down after World War II due to anti-Japanese hostility. It nearly disappeared as weeds and brush took over the unkempt land. But in recent decades, it was revived. Today, people like me are discovering the garden for the first time as they visit the Obama Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure In 2016, she spoke at its dedication in Chicago. “I'm working on the world peace, and I really think that we can make it,” Ono said.</p><h3><b>A cultural touchstone</b></h3><p>Today, the garden is what original caretaker Shoji Osato intended: a bridge between cultures. Michael Tanimura, chair of the Chicago Japanese American Council, first visited the Osaka Garden about 15 years ago. It’s become part of his Japanese American identity, realized only as an adult. When he was growing up in Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s, he just wanted to blend in as American.</p><p>Tanimura didn’t know much about his parents’ incarceration during World War II because they didn’t talk about it. “I never really thought to ask why, because it just was how things were and then I just accepted it,” he said.</p><p>In the 1990s, Tanimura learned more about their experience when his daughter interviewed his parents and relatives for a middle school project. “Even after knowing these things, I wasn't allowed to ask any questions of them,” he said.</p><div It gives her a touchstone for being Japanese.</p><p>“My granddaughter is always excited,” Tanimura said. “I'm sure it means something different to me than it does to her, but the advantage she has is she's actually getting that now at a young age, whereas I didn’t — or wasn't allowed to — actually feel and experience that until I was literally decades older.”</p><p>The Osaka Garden is a beautiful place to celebrate culture.
